# Field Service

`customer_support.model.field_service` · model · parent `—`

> Resolution requires a person to be physically present. That single constraint reorganises the whole domain, because it is the only branch where the scarce resource is not attention but location, and where the operating problem is scheduling rather than diagnosis. . Travel dominates everything. The marginal cost of a contact is geography, so a queue is not a list of tickets by urgency but a set of days that have already been quantised into visits, and a visit is unsplittable. Reassignment stops being a click: moving a job between technicians moves two people's routes and usually a customer's appointment. Prioritisation that ignores proximity produces schedules that look correct and cannot be driven. The same severity-one fault three hours away and forty minutes away are different jobs, and no amount of urgency changes that. . Parts are the second constraint and the dominant cost. A technician who arrives without the right component has burned a slot, a journey and the customer's morning, and has created a second appointment — the field-service equivalent of a reopen, and far more expensive. This is why first-time-fix rate, not first-contact resolution, is the metric the branch is actually run on, and why remote triage carries leverage that has no analogue elsewhere: every contact resolved over the phone avoids a cost measured in hundreds, not in minutes of handling time. . Third: the promise is an arrival window, not a response time. The customer took a day off. Being late here is not a slower version of the same failure — it consumed the customer's time rather than ours, and it is remembered as a different kind of broken promise. An SLA clock inherited from a ticketing branch measures the wrong thing entirely; what matters is whether somebody was standing there when they said they would be. . Fourth: the technician is alone with the customer, in their home or on their plant floor, unsupervised, and is the entire company for two hours. There is no transcript. Quality assurance has to be reconstructed from a job record written afterwards, by the person being assessed, frequently offline and hours later — and the record is thin exactly when the visit went badly. Access, safety and permits are preconditions no queue models: a job that cannot be entered, or where nobody is home, or where the site induction expired, is not a slow job, it is a cancelled one. . What an operator carries over wrongly from a remote desk: the belief that you can add capacity to a bad day. You cannot. Vans, certifications and driving hours are fixed weeks in advance, so an unexpected surge does not create a backlog that clears at the weekend — it creates appointments in three weeks' time, and the customer hears that number on the phone today. The second carry-over error is treating dispatch as routing: routing decides who, dispatch decides who and when and with what in the vehicle, and the third term is the one that fails.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | a site contact — homeowner, facilities manager, plant supervisor — who must be physically present for the visit and whose availability is a hard constraint on resolution, not a preference |
| typical_resolution_hours | 48 |
| volume_shape | low volume and very high unit cost, clustered geographically, strongly seasonal and weather-driven; a cold snap or a batch defect produces correlated demand in one region that no rota absorbs |
| staffing_model | dispatched field technicians with certifications and parts inventories, sitting behind a remote triage desk whose job is to prevent the visit |
| coverage | a service area before it is a service window — geography bounds what is possible, and an emergency call-out tier sits above the normal working day at a different price |
| automation_level | low at the point of work and high in scheduling; the automation that matters optimises routes and parts, not answers |
| primary_channels | `phone`, `ticket_portal`, `field_app`, `email` |
| notes | The record is written offline and late. Technicians work in basements, lifts, rural sites and plant rooms with no signal, so the job record is completed at the end of the day or the end of the week, and everything downstream — parts reconciliation, warranty claims, quality review, root cause on a recurring fault — inherits that lag. Designing the record for a tired person on a phone at 6pm is not a usability nicety in this branch; it is the difference between having field data and not having it.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.commitment`

Requires `due_at`, `due_specificity`, `notice_given`, `notice_given_at`


> The arrival window is the promise this branch is judged on, and it is a commitment with an unusual property: it binds the customer's time as well as ours. A four-hour window someone waited in and nobody arrived for is a worse event than a missed callback by a wide margin, and it is the only broken promise in the domain that costs the customer a day's pay. Proactive notification of slippage is worth more than the recovery, because the customer can still salvage the afternoon if told early enough.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.sla_target`

Requires `target_at`, `measured_from`, `calendar_type`, `is_contractual`


> `measured_from` carries the branch's whole disagreement with ticketing. The clock that matters starts when the job was booked and stops when a technician is on site — not at first response, which is trivially met by the triage desk and measures nothing about whether the fault stopped. Importing a response-time SLA into this branch produces excellent numbers and furious customers.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `assignee_ref`, `resolution_type`, `reopen_count`, `requester_ref`


> The assignee is a person with a location, a vehicle and a stock of parts, so assignment constrains what can physically be resolved rather than merely who will attempt it. `reopen_count` reads as revisits, which is the branch's dominant cost line and its cleanest quality signal — a revisit is nearly always a parts or diagnosis failure at the first visit, and almost never a customer misunderstanding.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `coverage_hours`, `plan`, `entitled_channels`


> The canonical entitlement object has no service-area attribute, and in this branch coverage is geographic before it is temporal — a contract that promises next-day attendance means something different at a site four hours from the nearest depot. This is a real gap in the shared object rather than a branch preference, and it is the first thing a field-service tenant will ask for. Until it exists, service area has to live in the coverage_hours prose, where nothing can compute against it.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`

Requires `working_hours`, `timezone`, `preferred_channel`


> Availability is a resolution constraint here, not a courtesy. A site contact who cannot be present on Tuesday makes Tuesday's slot unusable no matter how urgent the fault, and reaching them to confirm is on the critical path — an unreachable contact is the most common reason a technician's day loses an hour before it starts.

> This is the branch furthest from the shipped substrate. Nothing in Layer 1 or 2 emits a location, a route, a parts inventory or an appointment, so almost every reading this model depends on is pending — with one exception worth noting, which is that the arrival window is a commitment with a due_at and an action, and commitment_overdue therefore genuinely fires on the branch's single most important promise. That is the one real hook available today.
